Agreed 2026-09-04, revised 2026-09-05 with the price, the allowance numbers and
the soft-cap rule. **Nothing here is built.** This records the shape and the
reasoning so the decisions are not re-litigated, and so whoever implements it
knows which parts are settled and which are still open.

Supersedes the sketch in `monetization-direction` (session memory), which had
the meter as shopping trips alone.

---

## The shape, in one paragraph

Every feature is available to everybody. The free tier differs only in **how
much** you may do, expressed as **allowances** that visibly decrement. The user
is told where they stand before they run out, so hitting a limit is the end of a
countdown they were watching rather than a door slammed in their face. Paying
lifts the limits. Nothing is ever removed from an account that already has it.

---

## Settled

### No ads

Rejected, and the reasoning generalises: sessions are seconds long and this is a
shared family utility. There is no attention here to sell. The same argument
constrains our own messaging — see *The nudge* below.

### No feature gating

Every capability — camera, dictation, aisle mapping, all of it — works on the
free tier. A crippled free tier is what people judge the app on, and the AI is
the part that makes anyone want to pay for it. Gate the volume, never the
feature.

### A timed trial was considered and rejected

"Free for 30 days, then locked" takes the app away. An allowance never does: the
app keeps working, just less. People tolerate a smaller app far better than a
dead one, and a household grocery list that stops working strands two people
mid-week, not one.

### Two kinds of limit, presented separately

The status screen has two sections, and the difference is in the heading rather
than left to be inferred:

| Section | Heading reads | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Recurring** | "Resets in 12 days" | Aisle placements, parses |
| **Structural** | "Lifts when you subscribe" | Household members, total items |

"12 placements left" and "1 member slot left" look identical on a screen and
mean entirely different things — one refills on its own and one never will.
Labelling them the same way means people wait for the wrong number to reset.

The structural section doubles as the upgrade pitch: it is a list of exactly what
subscribing unlocks, sitting where somebody is already looking at their limits.

### Entitlement is per household, not per person

One member subscribes, the receipt is validated, and the **household** is marked
entitled on `householdId`. Every member benefits. This sidesteps Apple's
multi-user problem without Family Sharing.

Consequence for the copy: whoever hits a limit may not be whoever pays. The
message has to make sense to a person who cannot buy — "your household is out of
placements this month" — while offering the purchase to the person reading it.

### The period rolls from the household, not the calendar

Thirty days from household creation, rolled forward in 30-day steps. Somebody who
signs up on the 28th gets a full period, not three days. "Resets in N days" reads
the same either way, and it is one field on `Household` rather than a
system-wide clock. Decided 2026-09-05.

### One subscription, no one-off

**$1.99 a month or $14.99 a year.** Subscription only for the first version. The
"$0.99 to finish out the month" one-off is a good idea and is parked, not
rejected — a second SKU is a second thing to test, explain and validate, and one
SKU keeps the entitlement a boolean. Review once there is conversion data.

The price is derived in *The economics*, below. Short version: at $0.99 the free
tier loses money at any realistic conversion rate; at $1.99 it does not.

### Small Business Program

Enrol. Commission drops from 30% to 15%, which every figure in this document
assumes. Enrolment is by the Account Holder in App Store Connect after the Paid
Apps Agreement is signed; enrolling by the 15th of a month takes effect on the
1st of the next. Do it before the paywall ships, not after the first sale.

---

## The nudge

**The hard rule: never while `shoppingStatus == AT_STORE`.**

The app already distinguishes list-building at home from standing in a shop.
Asking somebody for money mid-shop is the one moment that turns a limit into
being held hostage, and it is the fastest way to make a household utility feel
predatory. This is an invariant, enforced in one place, not a judgement call at
each call site.

### Where it appears — settled 2026-09-05

Two places, and only two:

1. **On launch or return to foreground after a long background.** A pop-up
   showing where the household stands across every allowance. Bounded to launch,
   so it does not follow you around; a pop-up rather than a banner because he
   wants it read, not ignored. Threshold still open — see below.
2. **At the "I'm at the store" tap, before the state flips.** The app knows at
   that moment exactly what the trip will cost — the unmapped count is right
   there — so it can say "this trip uses 23 of your 30 placements" or "this is
   your last one." That is a warning about what is about to be spent, delivered
   before `AT_STORE`, and so consistent with the hard rule. Nothing is shown
   after the state flips.

**Why forewarning is the whole mechanism.** People resent surprise more than
restriction. An allowance that has been counting down in plain sight for a
fortnight is a fact; the same wall with no warning is an ambush. The reminders
are not marketing, they are what makes the limit acceptable.

**Threshold, settled 2026-09-05:** half or more of any recurring allowance
gone. Early in the period the number is noise and a dismiss on every launch
taxes an app opened several times a day to add one thing.

---

## The allowances

**"Allowance" is the word, everywhere** — in the code, in the UI and in this
document. Not "restriction", not "limit", not "quota". An allowance is something
you have; a restriction is something done to you, and the difference is the whole
tone of the free tier.

### The numbers — provisional, agreed 2026-09-05

Set against the baseline household described under *The economics*: two members,
two regular stores, a repertoire of about 150 products.

| Allowance | Kind | Free | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Aisle placements** | Recurring, soft | **100** | Month one for two stores needs ~300. 100 covers the first store's first trip (40–60) plus top-ups; a second store or a big first list crosses it. That is the nudge landing on the enthusiastic user, deliberately. Steady state (~15/month) never touches it |
| **Parses** | Recurring, soft | **3** | Recipe, paste, photo and dictation all count as one parse. The occasional user never notices; a meal-planner does. This is the only recurring cost on the free tier, so it is the tightest line |
| **Household members** | Structural | **2** | Two people shop in most households, so it rarely bites; the third is a genuine reason to pay |
| **Total items** | Structural | **150** | List and suggestions together. A typical repertoire fits; a big family's does not. Items cost nothing, so this is capacity, not metering |
| Photos | — | server cap only | 5 per item and 500 per household, enforced in the broker already. Not worth a line on the status screen |
| Shopping sessions | — | **none** | A session costs nothing. Metering it was pure friction with no cost story, and it was the one allowance that bit the normal case. Dropped 2026-09-05 |

### What the words are in the app

"Aisle placements" and "imports". A parse is an import to the person doing it —
the sheet is called Import, and paste, photo and dictation all land there — so
that is the word on the allowances page and in every refusal. "Parses" stays in
the code and the telemetry.

### Placements, not calls

The unit for aisle mapping is the **item placed in an aisle**, not the AI call. A
batch call places anywhere from one to fifty items; "12 calls left" tells the
user nothing about how many items that is. Placements are what they see on the
screen and what scales the bill.

### The cap is soft

**A trip that starts with allowance left is fully served.** The check is "is the
balance above zero"; if it is, the whole trip maps — all 23 items against 10
remaining — and the balance floors at zero. The next trip with nothing left shops
unmapped, under the **TO GET** heading that already exists for stores without
layouts. The trip proceeds either way; only the sorting stops.

Why soft rather than exact: an exact cap means mapping 10 of 23 and leaving the
list half-sorted, which needs an ordering rule and looks broken. The overshoot is
bounded by one trip's unmapped count, which is pennies. Same rule for parses —
the paste you just submitted parses in full even if it was your last one.

Decided 2026-09-05.

### Dictation is a parse

Dictation is recorded on device, transcribed by OpenAI (`gpt-4o-mini-transcribe`,
~$0.001 per clip), then handed to `parseIngredients` like any pasted text. The
transcription is not the cost; the parse behind it is. So a dictation is one
parse, and there is no separate dictation meter.

Apple's on-device recogniser (`SFSpeechRecognizer`, already used for the aisle
field) was never evaluated for list dictation — dictation arrived on Whisper in
`70d5cbc` with no comparison. Considered again 2026-09-05 and not pursued: the
saving is a tenth of a cent, offline transcription is worthless while the parse
still needs the network, and grocery vocabulary is where on-device accuracy is
weakest. The one real gain — one fewer external processor in the privacy policy —
only matters if the AWS-only posture in `APP-STORE-READINESS.qmd` goes ahead, and
that decision would justify the test on its own terms.

### One item allowance, not two

There is no separate suggestions cap, because there is no separate list.
`GroceryItem` is a single table with a status — `ACTIVE`, `IN_CART`,
`SUGGESTION` — and items move between them. The shopping list and the
suggestions are two views of one pool.

So the allowance is **total items in the household**, and it covers both by
construction. A suggestions cap smaller than the item cap would be incoherent
anyway: everything in suggestions arrived there from the list.

It also behaves like every other allowance — the wall refuses the next add, and
the user makes room by deleting. Nothing falls off on its own and nothing is
discarded behind their back.

### Comping an account

There must be a way to lift a household's allowances by hand, with no purchase —
friends, testers, people who helped. A flag on `Household` set by the admin
tooling, separate from any receipt, so the entitlement check reads
`subscribed || comped`.

Worth building at the same time as the paywall rather than after it: it is how
every allowance gets tested against a real account without buying anything.

### Two warnings carried forward from earlier decisions

**A shopping session is not an outing.** One trip to two shops finishes two
sessions — observed 2026-08-30. Sessions are no longer metered, so this no
longer sets a cap, but it still matters for reading usage data: 3–4 sessions a
week is a normal household, not a heavy one.

**A tight member cap was rejected on 2026-09-03, and reinstated on 2026-09-04.**
The original objection: a family of four is exactly who wants a shared list, and
a cap of two stops them experiencing why they would pay. The counter, which
carried: two people shop in most households, so a cap of two rarely bites at all,
and the third person is a clear and honest reason to pay rather than an
artificial one. It remains a poor *cost* proxy — five people shopping twice a
month cost less than two shopping daily — so it is sold as capacity, not as
metering.

### The wall must never eat work in progress

Hitting a limit refuses the **next** action. It never discards something
half-done, and it never fails a save that was already accepted. That is the
difference between a limit and a bug, and it is the one way this design could
make the app feel broken. The soft cap above is this rule applied to a trip.

---

## Implementation notes

### Two kinds of count

| Allowance | How it is known |
|---|---|
| Total items | **Derived.** Query `groceryItemsByHouseholdIdAndStatus` with `Select: COUNT` |
| Household members | **Derived.** Query `usersByHouseholdId` with `Select: COUNT` |
| Aisle placements | **Must be accumulated.** Not recorded anywhere today |
| Parses | **Must be accumulated.** Not recorded anywhere today |

Query the GSIs, never scan the table: a scan reads every household's rows to
count one household's, and it gets slower and dearer as the app grows.

### The two that need building

Neither leaves a row today. Both exist only as CloudWatch log lines, which
cannot answer "how many this period" per household at request time.

Simplest shape: counters on `Household` — `placementsThisPeriod`,
`parsesThisPeriod`, `periodStartedAt` — incremented with an atomic DynamoDB
`ADD` inside the Lambda that does the work, and reset lazily when
`periodStartedAt` is more than 30 days old. No scheduled job, no cron.
`periodStartedAt` is initialised to the household's creation time, which is what
makes the period roll from the household.

### Metered per household, attributed per user

Entitlement is per household, so the allowance is a **shared household pool**.
Metering per user would give a two-person household double the allowance and let
one member run dry while the other had plenty — of one shared list.

Record *who* spent each call as a telemetry field, not as a separate budget. It
answers "is one person doing all the mapping" without turning the pool into two.

### Enforcement is server-side — with one exception

The client check keeps the UI honest; the Lambda refusing is what makes the
allowance real. `inferProductAisle` and `parseIngredients` already call
`requireHousehold`, which is where the check belongs — same function, same
place, one more reason to refuse.

With a soft cap the server check is one comparison: balance above zero, serve
the whole request and `ADD` the count; otherwise refuse. The client's job is to
know the answer before asking, so the "at the store" warning can be shown.

A client-only check is not a limit, it is a suggestion.

**The exception is the item cap.** Items are written by the client straight
through `createGroceryItem`; there is no Lambda to refuse in. Enforcing 150 on
the server means routing every add through a custom mutation, a real lift for a
cap on something that costs nothing. Decided 2026-09-05: **client-only.** Known
consequence: a device that is offline (Paper List Mode) can add past 150 and
sync them up later. Accepted — the excess costs pennies, nothing is discarded,
and the next online add is refused as usual.

---

## Implementation plan — agreed 2026-09-05

Two phases. Phase 1 is everything except payment, tested on real accounts via
the comp flag; it goes through TestFlight and a release before Phase 2 starts.

### Phase 1 — backend

| Piece | Detail |
|---|---|
| `HouseholdAllowance` row | `placementsThisPeriod`, `parsesThisPeriod`, `periodStartedAt`, `entitlement` (`FREE`, `SUBSCRIBED`, `COMPED`), `subscriptionExpiresAt`. **Its own model, not fields on `Household`** — changed while building: members can update their own household row from the client, and a counter or entitlement flag a member can write is not a limit. The row is readable by the household (`groupDefinedIn`, read only) and written only by Lambdas over IAM, all through `amplify/data/allowance.ts`. Seeded when a household is created; created lazily on first metered use for households older than the table, whose period therefore starts at that first use |
| `householdAllowances` query | Returns balances **and caps**. Caps live in one server constants file; the client never hardcodes a number |
| `amplify/data/allowance.ts` | `checkAllowance(householdId, kind)`: load, lazily roll `periodStartedAt` in 30-day steps, refuse if `FREE` and balance ≤ 0. `spend(householdId, kind, n)`: atomic `ADD` **after** the work succeeds, so a failed Claude call is not charged. Entitled households are still counted, for telemetry |
| Wire in | `inferProductAisle` both modes, `n = results.length`; `parseIngredients`, `n = 1`. Both need `householdTable.grantReadWriteData` in `backend.ts` — the grant `householdMembership` already carries, so it should clear the nested-stack cycle that bit `itemImage`, but the deploy is the proof |
| Members | `joinHousehold` counts `usersByHouseholdId` (grant exists) and refuses the third unless entitled |
| Admin MCP | `comp_household`, `uncomp_household` |
| First act | Comp the live household. A separate test household exercises the free caps |

### Phase 1 — frontend

| Piece | Detail |
|---|---|
| `AllowanceService` | Fetches `householdAllowances` on launch, on return to foreground after **90 minutes**, and whenever the status screen opens. Cached in between |
| Launch pop-up | Only when half or more of any recurring allowance is gone. (The earlier "or 3 or fewer left" was dropped: with 3 free imports it would fire on every launch.) A system alert with the counts and "See allowances" / "OK" |
| `StoreSelectionSheet` | Before `showBatchMapping`: "this trip uses N of M", or "this is your last one"; at zero, skip the mapping sheet and go straight to At Store with the TO GET heading |
| `ShoppingListViewModel:2569` | Mid-trip mapping of items added from home. Handles the server refusal silently — it is `AT_STORE`, no nudge |
| `BulkImportSheet` | Same pre-check before parse; paste, photo and dictation share the path |
| Settings row | One row, `Plan · Free` / `Subscribed` / `Complimentary`, which opens the allowances page. Comped households are told they are comped — three states in the copy, decided 2026-09-05 |
| Allowances page | Plan label at the top, then the Recurring ("Resets in N days") and Structural ("Lifts when you subscribe") sections. An entitled household still sees its recurring counts, uncapped. Opening it refreshes. In Phase 2 the Subscribe button lives here and in the nudges, nowhere else |
| Item cap | Refused at 150 in `addItem` and the bulk-add paths. Client-only, see above |
| Refusal copy | The server's allowance error maps to the same wording everywhere, and always names when it resets |

### Phase 2 — payment

| Piece | Detail |
|---|---|
| StoreKit 2 | Two products, one `PaywallSheet`, reached only from the status screen and the nudges |
| `redeemSubscription` Lambda | Client sends the transaction JWS; the Lambda verifies Apple's signature and sets `entitlement = SUBSCRIBED` and `subscriptionExpiresAt` |
| Expiry | No webhook. The client re-syncs `Transaction.currentEntitlements` on launch and when the status screen opens, and re-redeems; the server treats a past `subscriptionExpiresAt` as `FREE`. A lapse is noticed at the next open, not the minute it happens — accepted |
| Small Business Program | Enrolled before this phase ships |

## The economics

::: {.callout-warning}
## Estimates, not measurements

There is no usage data — two developers testing is not usage. Every figure here
is derived from a **hypothetical baseline household**, agreed 2026-09-05, and
from published per-token prices. Use it for shape and for relative sizes. Replace
it with the structured telemetry once a handful of real households have shopped
for a fortnight.
:::

### Where the cost went — 2026-09-04 to 2026-09-05

The previous version of this section measured `inferProductAisle` on Sonnet
with a full sentence of `reasoning` per item, and recommended two levers before
pricing. **Both were pulled on 2026-09-05:** the model is `claude-haiku-4-5`
after a bake-off on the live Stop & Shop layout (Sonnet 29–30/31, Haiku 28/31,
at a third of the price), and `reasoning` is capped at ten words. The figures
below are for the app as it now runs.

### The baseline household

| | |
|---|---|
| Members on the app | 2, family of 3–4 |
| Sessions | ~3 a week: one big shop, two top-ups |
| Regular stores | 2 |
| Repertoire | ~150 distinct products by month three |
| List sizes | ~40 items on the big shop, ~8 on a top-up |
| Placements | ~300 in month one (150 products × 2 stores), ~15 a month after |
| Parses | ~3 a month, dictation included |
| Photos | ~10 a month |

### The shape: front-loaded, then near zero

A new household has an empty list and no stores. The first "I'm at the store"
tap maps most of the list at once — that is the bulk of the household's lifetime
AI spend, in one call. Each subsequent trip places only what is new, and the
list stabilises within a few weeks at one or two new items a trip. Mappings stay
with the store and are not redone. A second regular store restarts the hump once,
then it is flat again.

**The expensive user is the new user, not the heavy user.** A long-tenured
household that shops daily costs less than a fortnight-old one that shops weekly.
The only thing that does not decay is parsing, which is per action rather than
per item — a meal-planner pastes as many recipes in month twelve as in month
one. That is why parses carry the tightest free allowance.

This also means the recurring placement allowance binds hardest in month one and
stops binding by month three. That is accepted deliberately: hitting the wall
while enthusiastic — mid-onboarding, second store, big first list — is when
somebody is most willing to pay, and the soft cap means the wall never spoils
the trip they are on.

### Unit costs

Haiku 4.5 at $1 per Mtok in, $5 out.

| | Cost | How |
|---|---|---|
| One placement | **~$0.0005** | ~3k input tokens per batch (layout, existing mappings, items) shared across the batch; ~30 output tokens per item |
| One parse | **~$0.006** | Measured $0.005 input including cache write; ~300 output tokens |
| One dictation transcript | ~$0.001 | OpenAI, $0.003 per minute, ~20-second clips |
| Infrastructure | **~$0.03** per household per month | AppSync, DynamoDB, S3, Cognito at current volume. Cognito is free to 10,000 MAU |

Amplify build minutes (~$3 a month) and the Apple developer fee ($99 a year, about
eight yearly subscriptions) are fixed costs and are left out of the per-household
figures.

### Per household per month

| | Month one | Steady state |
|---|---|---|
| **Free**, at the caps (100 placements, 3 parses) | ~$0.10 | ~$0.06 |
| **Paid**, heavy (300 placements, 20 parses) | ~$0.30 | ~$0.15 |

A paying household covers its own cost many times over at any price considered.
That is not the question.

### The question is break-even conversion

The free tier is carried by the paid one. What matters is how many free
households one paid household can carry, and whether a realistic conversion
rate reaches that.

Net of 15% commission:

| Price | Net | Net per month | Free households carried at $0.06 | Break-even conversion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $0.99 / month | $0.84 | $0.84 | 14 | ~7% |
| $9.99 / year | $8.49 | $0.71 | 12 | **~8%** |
| **$1.99 / month** | $1.69 | $1.69 | 28 | ~3.5% |
| **$14.99 / year** | $12.74 | $1.06 | 18 | **~5%** |

Typical freemium conversion is 2–5%. At $0.99/$9.99 the yearly plan — which is
what most subscribers pick — needs 8%, at the far end of plausible. Worked at
3%: 100 households, 3 paying yield $2.13 a month, 97 free cost $5.82. A loss,
and one that grows with every free household.

At $1.99/$14.99 break-even is 3.5–5%, inside the normal range, and $14.99 a year
is what AnyList charges, so it is not an unfamiliar number. **Hence $1.99 a month,
$14.99 a year.** The yearly is priced at 7.5 months, the conventional discount.

Free parses were cut from a proposed 5 to 3 in the same pass: they are $0.03 of
the $0.06 steady-state free cost, the one line that does not decay with tenure,
and the difference between 5 and 3 is invisible to anyone who is not
meal-planning from recipes every week — who is exactly who should pay.

### What the infrastructure actually costs

Real bill, 30 days to 2026-09-04, by service:

| Service | 30 days |
|---|---|
| AWS Amplify | **$2.71** |
| AppSync | $0.028 |
| CloudWatch | $0.001 |
| Lambda | $0 |
| DynamoDB, S3, Cognito | not billed |

**The $2.71 is not a user cost.** Amplify bills build minutes — it is what
*deploying* costs, and it scales with how often `main` is pushed, not with how
many households exist.

Everything users actually touch came to **$0.03 a month.** A household that never
touches AI costs essentially nothing, which is why everything that is not an AI
call is either uncapped or capped only as capacity.

---

## Open questions

- The one-off "finish out the month" SKU — parked until there is conversion data.
- Whether a household that lapses keeps its data — it must, but the read-only
  behaviour needs specifying. With allowances rather than gates, "lapsed" most
  likely just means "back to free caps" with anything already over the cap kept
  and only the next add refused.
- Every number here, once there is a fortnight of real households in the
  telemetry.

## Prerequisites

- Per-household authorization — **done**, verified with an outsider account.
- Cost per household — **measurable**; the telemetry landed 2026-09-04. The
  estimates above get replaced by it.
- Small Business Program enrolment — not started; needs the Paid Apps Agreement.
- Phase 1 above — **built 2026-09-05, not yet deployed or tested.** Backend
  typechecks and existing tests pass; the app builds. Needs a push to deploy the
  schema, then the live household comped and a test household run through the
  caps.
- Phase 2 above — not started, and not before Phase 1 has shipped.
